exam: A patient with a fingertip injury cannot extend the distal phalanx – what is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management? — Identify mallet finger; splint in extension and arrange orthopedic review.

A 45‑year‑old with HIV presents with swollen DIP joint, fever, and a pustular skin lesion – what investigations and empiric therapy are indicated? — Joint aspiration, Gram stain, rapid HIV test; start IV ceftriaxone and consider anti‑TB if chronic.
How do you differentiate osteoarthritis from psoriatic arthritis of the DIP joint on exam? — Look for Heberden’s nodes (OA) versus nail pitting and skin plaques (psoriatic).

A child from a rural area has a painful DIP joint after stepping on a thorn; X‑ray is normal. What is your next step? — Suspect septic arthritis; perform joint aspiration if possible, start empirical antibiotics.
Why is a plain radiograph insufficient to rule out early septic arthritis of the DIP joint? — Early infection may not produce bony changes; clinical assessment and aspiration are essential.
What are the key components of splinting a mallet finger in a low‑resource setting? — Use a rigid card or plaster of Paris to keep the DIP in extension for 6‑8 weeks, educate on hygiene.
A patient with gout presents with a swollen DIP joint. Which bedside test helps confirm the diagnosis? — Perform joint aspiration for monosodium urate crystals; serum uric acid alone is insufficient.
When should you refer a patient with DIP joint deformity to surgery? — Persistent instability, severe deformity, or failure of conservative therapy after 3 months.
ai.title: Distal Interphalangeal Joint Disorders
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: The distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint is the hinge at the fingertip. Understanding its anatomy, common injuries, inflammatory diseases and tropical infections helps clinicians diagnose and manage pain, deformity and functional loss.

b: Extensor tendon insertion on the dorsal base of the distal phalanx
sections.p: The DIP joint is a synovial hinge between the distal phalanx and the middle phalanx. It allows flexion and extension of the fingertip and is covered by a thin articular cartilage and a fibroelastic capsule.

b: Infectious → septic arthritis, tuberculous arthritis, fungal (Candida) infection
sections.p: Clinicians must differentiate traumatic, inflammatory and infectious causes. In low‑resource settings, infections (e.g., mycobacterial or fungal) and delayed presentation of trauma are common.

b: Look for skin changes: pustules, psoriasis plaques
Check for systemic clues: fever, recent travel, HIV status
sections.p: Patients present with fingertip pain, swelling, limited motion or deformity. History of injury, systemic disease or exposure to soil/water guides the differential.

t.b: Is there a fracture, joint space narrowing or erosions? → Detect fractures, mallet deformity, osteophytes; if unavailable, use clinical criteria for fracture.
Is there purulent infection? → Positive Gram stain/culture confirms septic arthritis; if aspiration not possible, treat empirically if severe.
Is gout likely? → Elevated level supports gout but normal does not exclude; consider crystal analysis if possible.
Does immunosuppression predispose to atypical infection? → Positive test prompts broader antimicrobial coverage.

b: Fracture/dislocation → splint or reduction, refer for orthopedic care
Septic arthritis → urgent drainage, IV ceftriaxone (covers Staph) or anti‑TB drugs if TB suspected; avoid NSAIDs until infection ruled out
Osteoarthritis → hand therapy, splinting, topical NSAIDs; oral NSAIDs if tolerated
Psoriatic arthritis → methotrexate or sulfasalazine; avoid steroids alone as they may worsen skin disease
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then protect the joint and restore function.

b: Mallet finger: extensor tendon avulsion at DIP, no joint swelling
PIP arthritis: swelling proximal to DIP, different deformity pattern
sections.p: Mallet finger, proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint arthritis, and nail bed infections can mimic DIP pathology.

b: Early infection may have clear fluid but negative Gram stain; clinical suspicion overrides.
sections.p: Normal X‑ray does not exclude soft‑tissue injury; early septic arthritis may show no erosions.

b: Ask patient to flex/extend fingertip; pain at end range suggests DIP involvement
Inspect for nail changes—pitting points to psoriasis
Check for warmth and fluctuation indicating infection
sections.p: Focus on mechanism, systemic clues and simple bedside tests.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly increasing swelling, fever, or inability to move the finger – risk of joint destruction
Visible deformity after trauma – possible fracture/dislocation
Severe pain with systemic signs in an immunocompromised patient
